Trimi vs Shed: advertised prices, included services, and subscription terms compared

Compare Trimi and Shed by advertised GLP-1 prices, bundle inclusions, payment paths, automatic renewal, cancellation cutoffs, and refund boundaries.

Trimi and Shed make different commercial promises visible. Trimi's checked homepage leads with a compact flat-price bundle: compounded semaglutide at $99 per month and compounded tirzepatide at $125 per month on annual plans, with the same price at every dose. The page says one membership covers the medication, clinician visits, ongoing check-ins, and free shipping. Shed's product page presents a broader catalog and payment-path story, including insurance or cash-pay wording, branded and compounded options, and a pricing card that lists medication, supplies, member support, and shipping. Its price display is not one clean number. The checked page shows 'Starting at $149/month +' in one section, $199 per month in a later pricing card, and site banners advertising compounded semaglutide and tirzepatide at other figures. Shed's terms add another relevant layer by identifying $199 semaglutide and $299 tirzepatide as the current standard monthly rates after the minimum term for multi-month subscriptions. This page does not select the most favorable number. It records each context and tells the reader to verify the selected product, term, and cart before payment.

The contract evidence reverses the visibility pattern. Trimi's homepage clearly labels the lowest prices as annual-plan rates but does not publish the annual billing schedule, early-cancellation process, cutoff, or general refund calculation in the checked homepage content. That makes its bundle easy to understand at the headline level and incomplete at the commitment level. Shed's terms are much more explicit. They say medication programs renew automatically every 28 days or monthly depending on the program, impose a two-full-month minimum, and require cancellation at least 72 hours before the next billing date or scheduled shipment for the request to affect that cycle. General subscription fees are described as non-refundable once charged. The multi-month section says cancellation is available after the minimum term through the portal, an email cancellation link, or support; shipped cycles are treated as used; cancellation does not automatically trigger a refund; and an eligible amount for unfulfilled cycles may be calculated after used months are repriced at the applicable month-to-month rate. The terms also describe narrower exceptions. Those rules are commercially useful because they answer what happens after checkout. They do not prove that Shed's total is lower, that every plan uses the same cadence, or that a particular refund request will be approved.

Gala GLP-1 and Wellorithm appear only as benchmark context. Gala's checked page presents compounded GLP-1/GIP at $179 per month and labels the calculation as a yearly subscription plan; it also states that compounded GLP-1 is not FDA-approved. Wellorithm's checked page presents compounded semaglutide starting at $147 and compounded tirzepatide starting at $249, says no insurance is required, and includes free-shipping language. Neither benchmark receives ownership of this page, and neither price is treated as a quote for another plan. The Trimi-versus-Shed decision is narrower: a compact annual-plan bundle versus a multi-product offer backed by more visible subscription terms. Audit that obligation on a billing calendar: mark the enrollment timestamp, installment dates, renewal anniversary, shipment cycles, dispatch notices, prepaid balance, repricing formula, cancellation cutoff, submission proof, and acknowledgment email. Save the selected SKU, cart, invoice, courier identifier, card descriptor, and plan-length disclosure together. This catches timing exposure that an amortized monthly headline hides. There is no medical winner. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved, and FDA says they are not reviewed before marketing for safety, effectiveness, or quality. FDA recommends obtaining a prescription and using a state-licensed pharmacy. A licensed provider decides whether to prescribe. Prices, pharmacies, service areas, products, and terms can change after this July 23, 2026 check. Clinic Scout compares source-supported commercial evidence only; verify current terms directly.

Frequently asked questions

What is included in Trimi's advertised annual-plan price?
Trimi's checked homepage states $99 per month for compounded semaglutide and $125 per month for compounded tirzepatide on annual plans. It says the price stays the same at every dose and that one flat membership covers medication, clinician visits, ongoing check-ins, and free shipping. The annual-plan qualifier is part of the price, so compare the total commitment and billing schedule rather than multiplying an isolated monthly label without the checkout terms.
Does Trimi's homepage explain how to cancel the annual plan?
Not on the checked homepage. Trimi publishes annual-plan pricing, but the page reviewed for this comparison does not state the amount due at checkout, early-cancellation method, cutoff, refund calculation, or treatment of unshipped annual-plan orders. Its money-back statement points to separate terms and is tied to an outcome condition, so this page does not use that promotion as a recommendation or a general refund rule. Obtain the current plan terms before paying.
Why does this comparison show more than one Shed price?
The checked Shed product page is internally mixed. It shows a 'Starting at $149/month +' line, a separate pricing card at $199 per month with medication, supplies, support, and shipping, and site-level banners with other product-specific figures. Shed's terms then list current standard rates after a multi-month minimum term of $199 per month for compounded semaglutide and $299 per month for compounded tirzepatide. The only responsible comparison is to preserve the discrepancy and verify the selected product and checkout.
How does Shed describe automatic renewal and cancellation?
Shed's checked terms say medication programs automatically renew every 28 days or monthly depending on the program. They describe a minimum commitment of two full months and say cancellation is available after that minimum or at the close of the renewal cycle, whichever is longer. A cancellation must be submitted at least 72 hours before the next billing or shipment event to affect that cycle. Current-period charges remain due, and the cancellation generally stops future charges rather than reversing an existing one.
Does canceling Shed automatically produce a refund?
Shed's general subscription terms say charged subscription fees are non-refundable and list missed follow-ups, unused services, late cancellation, and cancellation before the minimum commitment among non-refund cases. Its multi-month section is more specific: cancellation does not itself create a refund, shipped cycles are used and non-refundable, and an eligible unfulfilled balance can be repriced at the month-to-month rate before a difference is returned. Exceptions and state-specific rights exist in the terms. This summary is not a promise that a refund applies.
Which provider is clearer about what the monthly payment buys?
Trimi's checked page is clearer on a single bundled annual-plan claim: product-specific monthly figures, no dose increase, medication, clinician visits, check-ins, and shipping in one statement. Shed discloses a wider product catalog, cash-pay or insurance wording, a pricing card that includes medication and supplies, member support, and shipping, plus a much more detailed subscription contract. Trimi has the cleaner public bundle headline; Shed has the deeper public recurring-term record. Those are commercial disclosure findings, not medical rankings.
Do the payment-path statements guarantee insurance or HSA/FSA reimbursement?
No. Trimi describes self-pay and HSA/FSA eligibility. Shed's product page mentions insurance or cash-pay options, while its terms also warn that insurance may not be accepted for Shed services. Neither statement binds an insurer or plan administrator. Confirm which entity bills each charge, whether the program fee, professional service, medication, supplies, or shipping are separate, and whether the exact expense is reimbursable before relying on insurance or tax-advantaged funds.
What should I save before choosing either subscription?
Capture the selected product page, cart, plan length, amount due now, billing cadence, renewal rate, cancellation method, cutoff, refund formula, shipment schedule, and all included or excluded charges. Ask which price applies when the page shows several figures. Keep the provider decision separate from the purchase decision: a licensed provider controls whether a prescription is issued, and the program can change availability. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. This comparison does not select a medication, estimate an outcome, assess individual safety, or decide eligibility.
